blocks.text: Adafactor is an optimizer specifically designed to reduce the memory overhead of Adam style optimizer state, covered in the earlier Optimizers topic, by factoring the large per parameter state into much smaller row and column summaries instead of storing a full estimate for every single parameter.
This topic explains the specific memory saving trick Adafactor uses, and when its tradeoffs make it a better fit than AdamW for a given fine-tuning project, particularly at very large model scale.
1. The Memory Problem Adafactor Solves

blocks.alt: Adam full per-parameter state leads to high memory usage at scale

blocks.text: Adam and AdamW, covered in the earlier Optimizers topic, maintain a running estimate for every single trainable parameter, which becomes a substantial memory cost at the scale of billions of parameters, exactly the kind of overhead the Optimizer States topic in this module covers in more general depth.
2. Factored Second Moment Estimates

blocks.alt: A full matrix second moment estimate gets replaced by row and column factors

blocks.text: Rather than storing a full estimate matching the shape of an entire weight matrix, Adafactor approximates that same information using much smaller row and column summary vectors, a mathematical factoring trick that captures most of the useful signal while using dramatically less memory.
3. How Adafactor Reduces Optimizer State Size

blocks.alt: Original matrix state gets factored into row and column vectors, using far less memory

blocks.text: For a weight matrix of size m by n, storing a full second moment estimate the same shape requires m times n values, while Adafactor factored approach needs only m plus n values, a dramatically smaller number, especially for the large matrices common in modern language models.

code.content:
# A conceptual comparison of memory needed
def full_state_size(rows, cols):
    return rows * cols

def factored_state_size(rows, cols):
    return rows + cols

print(full_state_size(4096, 4096))     # much larger
print(factored_state_size(4096, 4096)) # much smaller

blocks.text: 4. Adafactor vs Adam, The Core Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Adafactor uses less memory through factoring while Adam uses more memory with full state

blocks.text: Adafactor memory savings come at the cost of a less precise approximation of the true optimizer state Adam would maintain, a genuine tradeoff between memory efficiency and the exact adaptive behavior Adam provides, though in practice Adafactor has been shown to train large models effectively despite this approximation.

blocks.text: 5. Adafactor's Adaptive Learning Rate Behavior

blocks.alt: Parameter magnitude drives an adaptive step size

blocks.text: Adafactor also includes a built in mechanism for automatically scaling its effective learning rate relative to the magnitude of each parameter, in some configurations reducing or even eliminating the need to manually tune a separate learning rate schedule the way AdamW typically requires.
6. When Adafactor Is Worth Choosing

blocks.alt: A very large model with tight memory favors considering Adafactor

blocks.text: Adafactor is most worth considering specifically when fine-tuning very large models where even the reduced optimizer state overhead of a PEFT method, covered in earlier modules, still runs into memory pressure, since Adafactor further shrinks that specific overhead beyond what Adam or AdamW could achieve.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the earlier training on limited GPU discussion
blocks.content: Adafactor is one more tool in the same memory saving toolbox as quantization, LoRA, and gradient checkpointing, all covered earlier in this course, specifically targeting optimizer state rather than model weights or activations.

blocks.text: 7. Adafactor and Very Large Models

Adafactor was originally developed and popularized specifically for training extremely large models where Adam full state simply became impractical, and it remains a relevant choice today for fine-tuning projects operating at a similar scale, even though most smaller fine-tuning projects do fine with the more standard AdamW.
8. Limitations of Adafactor

blocks.alt: Adafactor can sometimes be trickier to tune than the more standard AdamW

blocks.text: Some practitioners have found Adafactor slightly trickier to get working well compared to the more thoroughly battle tested AdamW, with its automatic learning rate scaling behaving somewhat differently across tasks, making careful monitoring of the training loss curve especially important when using it.
9. Adafactor in Practice

Several widely used fine-tuning frameworks, covered further in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module later in this course, offer Adafactor as a selectable optimizer option, making it straightforward to try for a specific project without needing to implement its factoring mechanism from scratch.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a very large model finds that even with LoRA and quantization already applied, AdamW optimizer state for their still substantial number of trainable parameters pushes their memory usage right to the edge of what their hardware can handle.

Switching to Adafactor for the same training setup meaningfully reduces this specific overhead, giving them enough additional headroom to increase their batch size slightly, improving training stability without requiring any additional hardware.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing Adafactor by default for a small fine-tuning project where AdamW memory overhead was never actually a constraint
Not monitoring the loss curve closely when trying Adafactor for the first time, given its somewhat different tuning behavior
Assuming Adafactor and Adam produce identical training dynamics, when the factored approximation introduces real differences
Overlooking Adafactor specifically when optimizer state, rather than model weights, turns out to be the actual memory bottleneck

blocks.text: Practice

For a weight matrix of a size you choose, calculate the memory difference between storing full Adam style state versus Adafactor factored row and column state, confirming how much larger the savings become as the matrix grows.
Key Takeaway

Adafactor reduces optimizer state memory by factoring the large per parameter estimates Adam maintains into much smaller row and column summaries, a genuine memory versus precision tradeoff that makes it particularly valuable when fine-tuning very large models where even AdamW optimizer state overhead becomes a real constraint.
